requires.item: Sequentially Cohen-Macaulay modules (name only)

blocks.body:
Take the ring $k[x,y,z]$ of polynomial functions on 3-space and cut it down by one equation at a time: $x = 0$ leaves $k[y,z]$, then $y = 0$ leaves $k[z]$, then $z = 0$ leaves $k$, a point. Each cut lowers the dimension by one, as $n$ independent linear equations do in linear algebra. Now try the same on the ring $R = k[x,y]/(x^2,xy)$, which describes the $y$-axis with an extra infinitesimal "fuzz" at the origin. $R$ has dimension one, yet there is no good first cut through the origin: every polynomial $f$ vanishing at the origin kills the non-zero class of $x$, because $xf \in (x^2,xy)$. So $f$ is a zero-divisor, and dividing by it throws information away instead of cutting the space down cleanly.

Depth counts how many clean cuts are possible: it is the length of a longest regular sequence, a list of elements each of which is a non-zero-divisor on what the previous ones leave. Depth never exceeds dimension. A Cohen-Macaulay ring or module is one where the two agree: algebraically it behaves, as far as cutting by equations is concerned, like a smooth space, although it may be singular or even non-reduced. Macaulay (1916, polynomial rings) and Cohen (1946, power series rings) found the first instance: an ideal generated by as many elements as its height has no embedded components (the unmixedness theorem), and the rings with this property are exactly the Cohen-Macaulay rings.

This page defines regular sequences and depth, proves that depth is the first non-vanishing $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)$, proves the depth lemma and the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula, and then develops Cohen-Macaulay modules: their characterisations (systems of parameters, freeness over a polynomial subring), their localisations, the height and unmixedness theorems, maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules, Serre's conditions $(S_n)$, and a glimpse of Gorenstein rings, local cohomology and Stanley-Reisner rings. Research papers use all of this as background: Holanda and Miranda-Neto assume modules are maximal Cohen-Macaulay to get freeness criteria, Guan and Hu formalise depth and Cohen-Macaulay rings in Lean, Iyengar, Ma, Schwede and Walker read depth off local cohomology and Koszul complexes, and combinatorial papers decide Cohen-Macaulayness of monomial ideals. Throughout, rings are commutative and Noetherian, $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ denotes a local ring ([[local-rings]]), and modules are finitely generated unless said otherwise.

blocks.title: Regular sequences
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to decide whether a given list of elements is a regular sequence on a module, and you will know when the order of the list matters.

A non-zero-divisor on an $R$-module $M$ is an $x\in R$ such that $xa = 0$ with $a\in M$ forces $a = 0$; equivalently multiplication $M\xrightarrow{x}M$ is injective. Hochster describes a regular sequence as a list of "independent" equations: each new element is a non-zero-divisor on whatever the earlier ones have left, so each step cuts the module down as far as one equation can. In $k[x,y,z]$ the sequence $x,y,z$ has this property, since $x$ is a non-zero-divisor on $k[x,y,z]$, then $y$ on $k[x,y,z]/(x)\cong k[y,z]$, then $z$ on $k[z]$.

blocks.title: Regular and weakly regular sequences
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be an $R$-module. A sequence $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of elements of $R$ is $M$-regular if

1. for each $i$, $x_i$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M/(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1})M$ (for $i = 1$ this module is $M$), and
2. $M/(x_1,\dots,x_n)M\neq0$.

A sequence satisfying only condition 1 is called weakly regular by Guan and Hu (following Mathlib) and possibly improper regular by Hochster. The empty sequence is $M$-regular exactly when $M\neq0$.

If $(R,\mathfrak m)$ is local, $M$ is finitely generated and non-zero, and all $x_i$ lie in $\mathfrak m$, then condition 2 is automatic: $(x_1,\dots,x_n)M\subseteq\mathfrak mM\neq M$ by Nakayama's lemma ([[local-rings]]). This is why Weibel, who works over a local ring, defines a regular sequence by condition 1 for elements of $\mathfrak m$ alone.

blocks.title: First regular sequences
blocks.body:
Decide which of the following are regular sequences.

1. $6,35$ and $6,4$ on $M = \mathbb Z$.
2. $x,y$ and $x^2, y^2$ on $k[x,y]$.
3. $x$ and $x+y$ on $R = k[x,y]/(xy)$, and whether $x+y$ can be extended by a second element of $(x,y)$.
4. Any non-empty sequence in $(x)$ on $R = k[x]/(x^2)$.
blocks.solution:
1. $6$ is a non-zero-divisor on $\mathbb Z$. On $\mathbb Z/6$ multiplication by $35\equiv5$ is bijective, so condition 1 holds, but $\mathbb Z/(6,35) = 0$ because $\gcd(6,35) = 1$. So $6,35$ is weakly regular but not regular. For $6,4$: $4\cdot3 = 12\equiv0$ in $\mathbb Z/6$ while $3\not\equiv0$, so $4$ is a zero-divisor on $\mathbb Z/6$ and condition 1 fails.

2. $x$ is a non-zero-divisor on the domain $k[x,y]$; $k[x,y]/(x)\cong k[y]$ is a domain on which $y$ acts as a non-zero element, so $y$ is a non-zero-divisor; and $k[x,y]/(x,y) = k\neq0$. For $x^2,y^2$: $x^2\neq0$ in a domain; $k[x,y]/(x^2)$ has $k[y]$-basis $1, x$, and multiplication by $y^2$ sends $a(y)+b(y)x$ to $y^2a(y)+y^2b(y)x$, which is zero only if $a = b = 0$; and the quotient $k[x,y]/(x^2,y^2)$ has $k$-basis $1,x,y,xy$, so it is non-zero.

3. $x$ is a zero-divisor, since $x\cdot y = 0$ and $y\neq0$ in $R$. For $x+y$: every element of $R$ can be written uniquely as $f = c+xp(x)+yq(y)$ with $c\in k$ and polynomials $p,q$ (the monomials not divisible by $xy$ form a basis). Then $(x+y)f = cx+cy+x^2p(x)+y^2q(y)$, which is zero only if $c = 0$, $p = 0$, $q = 0$. So $x+y$ is a non-zero-divisor. The quotient is $R/(x+y)\cong k[x]/(x^2)$ (substitute $y = -x$, then $xy = -x^2$), which is non-zero. In $k[x]/(x^2)$ every element of $(x)$ kills $x\neq0$, so no element of $(x,y)$ is a non-zero-divisor on $R/(x+y)R$, and $x+y$ cannot be extended inside $(x,y)$.

4. Every element of $(x)\subseteq k[x]/(x^2)$ has the form $ax$ and kills $x\neq0$. So no non-empty sequence in $(x)$ is regular; only the empty sequence is.

blocks.title: Recall: associated primes
blocks.body:
Regular sequences are controlled by associated primes, which belong to their own page (associated primes and primary decomposition); we only recall the facts used here, with proofs in the Stacks Project, §10.63. A prime $\mathfrak p$ is associated to $M$ if $\mathfrak p = \operatorname{Ann}(a)$ for some $a\in M$; the set is $\operatorname{Ass}M$. The support is $\operatorname{Supp}M = \{\mathfrak p: M_{\mathfrak p}\neq0\}$, which equals $V(\operatorname{Ann}M)$ for finitely generated $M$ ([[localization]]). For $R$ Noetherian and $M$ finitely generated:

1. $\operatorname{Ass}M$ is finite, and non-empty if $M\neq0$.
2. The set of zero-divisors on $M$ is the union of the associated primes of $M$.
3. $\operatorname{Ass}M\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}M$, and the minimal elements of $\operatorname{Supp}M$ (the primes minimal over $\operatorname{Ann}M$) are associated. Associated primes that are not minimal are called embedded.
4. For a multiplicative set $S$, $\operatorname{Ass}(S^{-1}M)$ consists of the $S^{-1}\mathfrak p$ with $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$ and $\mathfrak p\cap S = \varnothing$. In particular $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$ if and only if $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}\in\operatorname{Ass}M_{\mathfrak p}$.

Combined with prime avoidance (an ideal contained in a finite union of primes lies in one of them), facts 1 and 2 give the form in which they are used below: if every element of an ideal $I$ is a zero-divisor on $M$, then $I\subseteq\mathfrak p$ for some $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$, so $I$ kills some $a\neq0$. Weibel records the case $I = \mathfrak m$ as one of his standard facts 4.4.7: if every element of $\mathfrak m$ is a zero-divisor on $M\neq0$, then $\mathfrak m = \operatorname{Ann}(a)$ for some $a\in M$.

blocks.title: What a regular sequence is
blocks.body: Three explanations of the same notion.

items.label: Independent equations
items.body: Hochster's reading: each new element is a non-zero-divisor on what the earlier ones leave, so no equation is a consequence of, or entangled with, the previous ones; dividing by it loses nothing except what it is meant to cut away.

items.label: Dimension drops by one
items.body: Geometrically, cutting $M$ by a regular element $x\in\mathfrak m$ lowers the dimension by exactly one: $\dim M/xM = \dim M-1$ (Guan-Hu Lemma 2.3; Weibel 4.4.7 for $M = R$). A regular sequence of length $n$ lowers it by $n$, like $n$ independent hyperplanes; the converse fails in general and holds exactly for Cohen-Macaulay modules.

items.label: Exact Koszul complex
items.body: Homologically, $x_1,\dots,x_n$ regular on $M$ makes the Koszul complex $K(x;M)$ exact except in degree $0$, where its homology is $M/(x)M$ (Weibel Corollary 4.5.4). For $M = R$ the Koszul complex is then a free resolution of $R/(x)$, as for $x,y$ in $k[x,y]$ on [[tor]].

blocks.title: Permuting a regular sequence
blocks.body: Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring, $M$ a finitely generated module, and $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\mathfrak m$ an $M$-regular sequence. Then every permutation of $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is $M$-regular. (Stacks Lemma 10.68.4; Hochster proves the same in the local and in the graded case.)

Every permutation is a product of transpositions of neighbours, and swapping $x_i,x_{i+1}$ only affects the conditions at steps $i$ and $i+1$, which concern the module $N = M/(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1})M$. Condition 2 holds by Nakayama's lemma. So it suffices to show: if $x,y\in\mathfrak m$ and $x,y$ is $N$-regular for a finitely generated $N$, then $y,x$ is $N$-regular.

$y$ is a non-zero-divisor on $N$. Let $K = \{a\in N: ya = 0\}$. If $a\in K$, then $y\bar a = 0$ in $N/xN$, so $\bar a = 0$ because $y$ is a non-zero-divisor on $N/xN$; thus $a = xb$ for some $b\in N$. Then $x(yb) = y(xb) = 0$, and since $x$ is a non-zero-divisor on $N$, $yb = 0$, i.e. $b\in K$. Hence $K = xK$. $K$ is finitely generated (a submodule of a finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring) and $x\in\mathfrak m$, so $K = 0$ by Nakayama's lemma.

$x$ is a non-zero-divisor on $N/yN$. Let $xa\in yN$, say $xa = yb$. Then $y\bar b = 0$ in $N/xN$, so $b = xc$ for some $c$. Hence $x(a-yc) = 0$, so $a = yc\in yN$.

blocks.title: Order matters away from the local case
blocks.body: In $A = k[x,y,z]$ the Stacks Project (Example 10.68.2) notes that $x,\ y(1-x),\ z(1-x)$ is $A$-regular. Show that $y(1-x),\ z(1-x),\ x$ is not, and that it becomes regular in the local ring $A_{\mathfrak m}$, $\mathfrak m = (x,y,z)$.
blocks.solution:
First the regular one: $A/(x)\cong k[y,z]$, on which $y(1-x)$ acts as $y$, a non-zero-divisor; $A/(x,y(1-x)) = A/(x,y)\cong k[z]$, on which $z(1-x)$ acts as $z$; and $A/(x,y,z) = k\neq0$.

For $y(1-x), z(1-x), x$: in $A/(y(1-x))$ the class of $y$ is not zero, since $y = y(1-x)g$ would force $(1-x)g = 1$, impossible by degrees. But $z(1-x)\cdot y = z\cdot y(1-x)\in(y(1-x))$. So $z(1-x)$ is a zero-divisor on $A/(y(1-x))$.

In $A_{\mathfrak m}$ the element $1-x\notin\mathfrak m$ is a unit, so the ideals $(y(1-x))$ and $(y)$ agree, as do $(y(1-x),z(1-x))$ and $(y,z)$; multiplying an element by a unit does not change whether it is a non-zero-divisor. So the sequence is regular in $A_{\mathfrak m}$ if and only if $y,z,x$ is, and $y,z,x$ is $A$-regular (quotients $k[x,z]$, $k[x]$, $k$) and stays regular after localising at $\mathfrak m$ by the theorem below. This is consistent with the permutation theorem: $x,y,z$ is regular in the local ring $A_{\mathfrak m}$, so every permutation is.

blocks.title: Regular sequences under localisation
blocks.body:
Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be $M$-regular and $S\subseteq R$ multiplicative.

1. Each $x_i/1$ is a non-zero-divisor on $S^{-1}M/(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1})S^{-1}M$, so $x_1/1,\dots,x_r/1$ is weakly $S^{-1}M$-regular.
2. If $M$ is finitely generated, $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Supp}M$ and all $x_i\in\mathfrak p$, then $x_1/1,\dots,x_r/1$ is $M_{\mathfrak p}$-regular.

(Guan and Hu formalise part 1 for flat base change and add part 2 separately, since $R\to R_{\mathfrak p}$ is flat but not faithfully flat.)

Localisation is exact and $S^{-1}(IM) = (S^{-1}I)(S^{-1}M)$, so $S^{-1}(M/I_{i-1}M)\cong S^{-1}M/I_{i-1}S^{-1}M$ for $I_{i-1} = (x_1,\dots,x_{i-1})$. Injectivity of $x_i$ on $M/I_{i-1}M$ is the exactness of $0\to M/I_{i-1}M\xrightarrow{x_i}M/I_{i-1}M$, which survives localisation; this is part 1. For part 2 only condition 2 remains: $M_{\mathfrak p}\neq0$ is finitely generated over the local ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$, and $(x_1,\dots,x_r)M_{\mathfrak p}\subseteq\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}M_{\mathfrak p}\neq M_{\mathfrak p}$ by Nakayama's lemma. Without $x_i\in\mathfrak p$ this fails: $2$ is $\mathbb Z$-regular, but $\mathbb Z_{(3)}/2\mathbb Z_{(3)} = 0$.

items.q: Is $2$ a regular sequence on $\mathbb Z/4$? On $\mathbb Z/3$?
items.a: Not on $\mathbb Z/4$: $2\cdot2 = 0$. On $\mathbb Z/3$, $2$ is a non-zero-divisor but $\mathbb Z/(3,2) = 0$, so it is only weakly regular.

items.q: Over a local ring, can condition 2 fail for a non-zero finitely generated $M$ and elements of $\mathfrak m$?
items.a: No: by Nakayama's lemma $(x_1,\dots,x_n)M\subseteq\mathfrak mM\neq M$.

items.q: An ideal $I$ consists of zero-divisors on a finitely generated $M\neq0$. What can you conclude?
items.a: $I$ lies in an associated prime of $M$, so some $a\neq0$ in $M$ satisfies $Ia = 0$ (finiteness of $\operatorname{Ass}M$ plus prime avoidance).

items.q: Why does the permutation theorem not contradict the example $y(1-x),z(1-x),x$ in $k[x,y,z]$?
items.a: The theorem needs a local ring and elements of its maximal ideal; $k[x,y,z]$ is not local, and $1-x$ is a unit only after localising at $(x,y,z)$.

items.q: In $\mathbb Z$, decide whether $4,9$ and $4,6$ are regular, weakly regular, or neither.
items.hint: Look at the action of the second element on $\mathbb Z/4$ and at the final quotient.
items.solution: On $\mathbb Z/4$, $9\equiv1$ acts bijectively, so $4,9$ satisfies condition 1, but $\mathbb Z/(4,9) = 0$: weakly regular, not regular. For $4,6$: $6\cdot2 = 12\equiv0$ in $\mathbb Z/4$ with $2\neq0$, so $6$ is a zero-divisor on $\mathbb Z/4$: neither.

items.q: Show that $x^2,y^2$ is $k[x,y]$-regular and that $\dim_k k[x,y]/(x^2,y^2) = 4$. Is $y^2,x^2$ regular as well?
items.hint: Use the $k[y]$-basis $1,x$ of $k[x,y]/(x^2)$.
items.solution: Done in the worked example: $x^2$ is a non-zero-divisor on the domain $k[x,y]$; on $k[x,y]/(x^2) = k[y]\oplus k[y]x$ multiplication by $y^2$ is injective componentwise; and $k[x,y]/(x^2,y^2)$ has basis $1,x,y,xy$, so dimension $4$. By symmetry (exchange $x$ and $y$) the sequence $y^2,x^2$ is regular too; this is also an instance of the permutation theorem after localising at $(x,y)$.

items.q: Let $R$ be Noetherian, $M$ finitely generated and $I$ an ideal with $IM\neq M$. Show that $I$ contains an $M$-regular element if and only if $I\not\subseteq\mathfrak p$ for every $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$.
items.hint: Zero-divisors form the union of the associated primes, which is a finite union.
items.solution:
An element $x\in I$ is $M$-regular exactly when it is a non-zero-divisor on $M$ (condition 2 holds since $xM\subseteq IM
eq M$), i.e. when $x
otin igcup_{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M}\mathfrak p$. If $I\subseteq\mathfrak p$ for some associated $\mathfrak p$, every element of $I$ is a zero-divisor. Conversely, if $I$ consisted of zero-divisors, then $I\subseteq igcup_{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M}\mathfrak p$, a finite union of primes, and by prime avoidance $I\subseteq\mathfrak p$ for one of them. So $I
ot\subseteq\mathfrak p$ for all associated $\mathfrak p$ forces an $M$-regular element in $I$.

items.q: Let $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ be an exact sequence of $R$-modules and $y\in R$ a non-zero-divisor on $A$ and on $C$. Show that $y$ is a non-zero-divisor on $B$ and that $0\to A/yA\to B/yB\to C/yC\to0$ is exact.
items.hint: Apply the snake lemma to multiplication by $y$ on the sequence.
items.solution: Multiplication by $y$ gives a map of the short exact sequence to itself. The snake lemma yields an exact sequence $$\begin{aligned}&0\to\ker_A\to\ker_B\to\ker_C\\ &\quad\to A/yA\to B/yB\to C/yC\to0,\end{aligned}$$ where $\ker_X$ is the kernel of $y$ on $X$. Since $\ker_A = \ker_C = 0$, also $\ker_B = 0$, so $y$ is a non-zero-divisor on $B$, and the connecting map starts from $\ker_C = 0$, so $0\to A/yA\to B/yB\to C/yC\to0$ is exact.

items.q: Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, $M$ finitely generated, and $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\mathfrak m$ an $M$-regular sequence. Show that $x_1^{a_1},\dots,x_n^{a_n}$ is $M$-regular for all $a_i\ge1$.
items.hint: By the permutation theorem it suffices to replace $x_1$ by $x_1^a$. Induct on $a$ using $0\to M/x_1M\to M/x_1^aM\to M/x_1^{a-1}M\to0$, where the first map is multiplication by $x_1^{a-1}$, and the previous exercise.
items.solution:
Step 1: it suffices to show that $x_1^a,x_2,\dots,x_n$ is $M$-regular for every $a\ge1$. Indeed, then replace the elements one at a time: to raise $x_j$ to a power, permute $x_j$ to the front (permutation theorem), raise it, and permute back.

Step 2: the exact sequence. Write $N_a = M/x_1^aM$. Since $x_1$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M$, so is $x_1^a$. The map $N_1\to N_a$, $\bar m\mapsto\overline{x_1^{a-1}m}$, is well defined ($x_1M$ goes to $x_1^aM$) and injective: if $x_1^{a-1}m = x_1^am'$ then $x_1^{a-1}(m-x_1m') = 0$, so $m = x_1m'$. Its image is $x_1^{a-1}M/x_1^aM$, with cokernel $N_{a-1}$. So $0\to N_1\to N_a\to N_{a-1}\to0$ is exact.

Step 3: induction on $a$, the case $a = 1$ being the hypothesis. Assume $x_2,\dots,x_n$ satisfies condition 1 on $N_{a-1}$, and it does on $N_1$ by hypothesis. Apply the previous exercise with $y = x_2$: $x_2$ is a non-zero-divisor on $N_a$, and the reduction modulo $x_2$ of the sequence, $$0\to\tfrac{N_1}{x_2N_1}\to\tfrac{N_a}{x_2N_a}\to\tfrac{N_{a-1}}{x_2N_{a-1}}\to0,$$ is exact. Repeat with $x_3$ on this sequence, and so on up to $x_n$. This gives condition 1 for $x_2,\dots,x_n$ on $N_a$, hence for $x_1^a,x_2,\dots,x_n$ on $M$. Condition 2 holds by Nakayama's lemma since all elements lie in $\mathfrak m$.

blocks.body:
- An $M$-regular sequence: each $x_i$ is a non-zero-divisor modulo the earlier ones, and $M/(x_1,\dots,x_n)M\neq0$; without the last condition it is weakly regular.
- Over a local ring with $x_i\in\mathfrak m$ the last condition is automatic (Nakayama), and regular sequences can be permuted.
- Away from the local case the order matters: $x,y(1-x),z(1-x)$ versus $y(1-x),z(1-x),x$.
- An ideal $I$ contains a non-zero-divisor on $M$ unless $I$ lies in an associated prime of $M$.
- Regular sequences inside $\mathfrak p$ stay regular in $R_{\mathfrak p}$.

blocks.title: Depth
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to compute the depth of a module, either by finding a regular sequence that cannot be extended or by computing $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)$, and you will know why depth is at most the dimension.

In the example $R = k[x,y]/(xy)$ above, the element $x+y$ was regular and could not be extended. Could a cleverer first choice have produced a longer sequence? The answer is no: all regular sequences in a given ideal that cannot be extended have the same length. The proof goes through Ext ([[ext]]), and in particular through the computation made there for a non-zero-divisor $x$: from the resolution $0\to R\xrightarrow{x}R\to R/xR\to0$ one gets $\mathrm{Ext}^0(R/xR,M) = \{a\in M: xa = 0\}$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/xR,M)\cong M/xM$. Bruns and Herzog open their book with depth for this reason: after dimension it is the most fundamental numerical invariant of a local ring or a module, defined by regular sequences but detected by Ext and by the Koszul complex.

blocks.title: Depth
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be Noetherian, $I$ an ideal and $M$ a finitely generated module with $IM\neq M$. The $I$-depth $\operatorname{depth}_IM$ (also called the grade of $I$ on $M$) is the supremum of the lengths of $M$-regular sequences in $I$. If $IM = M$, one sets $\operatorname{depth}_IM = \infty$.

For a local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$, the depth of $M$ is $\operatorname{depth}M = \operatorname{depth}_{\mathfrak m}M$. By Nakayama's lemma $\mathfrak mM\neq M$ for $M\neq0$, so $\operatorname{depth}M$ is defined by regular sequences for every non-zero $M$, and the convention gives $\operatorname{depth}0 = \infty$. We write $\operatorname{depth}R$ for the depth of $R$ as a module over itself.

Examples: $\operatorname{depth}\mathbb Z_{(p)} = 1$ ($p$ is regular, and $\mathbb Z_{(p)}/p$ is a field, on which $p$ acts as $0$); $\operatorname{depth}k[x]/(x^2) = 0$; and the localisation of $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ at $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ has depth at least $n$, since $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is regular. The theorems below show that this last depth is exactly $n$.

blocks.title: Depth is the first non-vanishing Ext
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be Noetherian, $I$ an ideal, and $M$ finitely generated with $IM
eq M$. Let $x_1,\dots,x_n\in I$ be an $M$-regular sequence that cannot be extended by an element of $I$. Then
$$\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(R/I,M) = 0\ \ (i<n),\qquad \mathrm{Ext}^n_R(R/I,M)
eq0.$$
Consequently all non-extendable $M$-regular sequences in $I$ have the same length, every $M$-regular sequence in $I$ extends to one of this length, and
$$\operatorname{depth}_IM = \min\{i:\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(R/I,M)
eq0\}<\infty.$$
For $R$ local and $M
eq0$ this reads $\operatorname{depth}M = \min\{i:\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(k,M)
eq0\}$. (Weibel Theorem 4.4.8 for $I = \mathfrak m$; Stacks Lemma 10.72.5; Rees's theorem in the form of Ogus, Theorem 0.2(2), and Guan-Hu, Theorem 3.1.)

Idea: induct on $n$, dividing by $x_1$; multiplication by $x_1$ is injective on $M$ but induces zero on every $\mathrm{Ext}^i(R/I,-)$, so the long exact sequence breaks into short pieces and shifts the vanishing range by one.

Two observations. (a) If some $x\in I$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M$, then $\mathrm{Hom}(R/I,M) = 0$: a homomorphism $R/I\to M$ sends $1$ to some $a$ with $Ia = 0$, so $xa = 0$ and $a = 0$. (b) For $x\in I$, the map $\mathrm{Ext}^i(R/I,M)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(R/I,M)$ induced by multiplication by $x$ on $M$ is multiplication by $x$ on the $R$-module $\mathrm{Ext}^i(R/I,M)$, which is killed by $\operatorname{Ann}(R/I) = I$ ([[ext]], module structure). So it is zero.

Base case $n = 0$: no element of $I$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M$, so by the recalled facts on associated primes $I\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}(a)$ for some $a\neq0$, and $1\mapsto a$ is a non-zero homomorphism $R/I\to M$. So $\mathrm{Ext}^0(R/I,M)\neq0$.

Induction step $n\ge1$: put $x = x_1$ and $\bar M = M/xM$. Then $I\bar M\neq\bar M$, because $\bar M/I\bar M = M/IM$. The sequence $x_2,\dots,x_n$ is $\bar M$-regular and cannot be extended in $I$ (an extension would extend $x_1,\dots,x_n$). By induction $\mathrm{Ext}^i(R/I,\bar M) = 0$ for $i<n-1$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^{n-1}(R/I,\bar M)\neq0$. Apply $\mathrm{Hom}(R/I,-)$ to $0\to M\xrightarrow{x}M\to\bar M\to0$. By (b) every map induced by $x$ in the long exact sequence is zero, so it splits into short exact sequences
$$0\to E^i(M)\to E^i(\bar M)\to E^{i+1}(M)\to0\qquad(i\ge0),$$
writing $E^i = \mathrm{Ext}^i(R/I,-)$. For $i<n-1$ the middle term vanishes, so $E^{i+1}(M) = 0$; with $E^0(M) = 0$ from (a) this gives $E^j(M) = 0$ for all $j\le n-1$. For $i = n-1$ the left term is then zero, so $E^n(M)\cong E^{n-1}(\bar M)\neq0$.

Conclusion. The length of a non-extendable sequence equals $\min\{i: E^i(M)\neq0\}$, which does not depend on the sequence. Every $M$-regular sequence in $I$ can be extended until it cannot be extended further: if $x_{i+1}$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M/(x_1,\dots,x_i)M\neq0$ then $x_{i+1}\notin(x_1,\dots,x_i)$, since elements of that ideal kill the quotient; so the ideals $(x_1,\dots,x_i)$ increase strictly, and as $R$ is Noetherian the process stops. Condition 2 never fails along the way, because $(x_1,\dots,x_i)M\subseteq IM\neq M$. Hence no regular sequence in $I$ is longer than $n$, and the supremum defining the depth is this minimum.

blocks.title: Depth drops by one modulo a regular element
blocks.body:
In the situation of the theorem, let $x\in I$ be $M$-regular. Then $\operatorname{depth}_I(M/xM) = \operatorname{depth}_IM-1$, and
$$\mathrm{Ext}^{n}_R(R/I,M)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{n-1}_R(R/I,M/xM)\quad(n = \operatorname{depth}_IM).$$
In particular, for $R$ local, $x\in\mathfrak m$ $M$-regular: $\operatorname{depth}M/xM = \operatorname{depth}M-1$. (Stacks Lemma 10.72.7; Guan-Hu Theorem 3.6.)

Extend $x$ to a non-extendable $M$-regular sequence $x,x_2,\dots,x_n$ in $I$; by the theorem $n = \operatorname{depth}_IM$. Then $x_2,\dots,x_n$ is a non-extendable $M/xM$-regular sequence in $I$, of length $n-1$, so $\operatorname{depth}_I(M/xM) = n-1$. The isomorphism is the one found in the induction step of the previous proof.

blocks.title: Depth of the node, twice
blocks.body: Let $R$ be $k[x,y]/(xy)$ localised at $(x,y)$, the local ring of two crossing lines. Compute $\operatorname{depth}R$ from a regular sequence, then confirm it with Ext.
blocks.solution:
Regular sequence. In the example of the previous section (whose computation is unchanged by localising) $x+y$ is $R$-regular and $R/(x+y)\cong k[x]/(x^2)$, localised, in which every element of the maximal ideal kills $x\neq0$. So $x+y$ cannot be extended, and $\operatorname{depth}R = 1$ by the theorem.

Ext. $\mathrm{Hom}(k,R)$ is the socle $\{f: xf = yf = 0\}$. If $xf = 0$ and $yf = 0$ in $R$, then in $k[x,y]$ the element $f$ lies in $(xy):x = (y)$ and in $(xy):y = (x)$, hence in $(x)\cap(y) = (xy)$, so $f = 0$. Thus $\mathrm{Ext}^0(k,R) = 0$. By the isomorphism of the last theorem with $x+y$, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(k,R)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(k,R/(x+y)R)$, the socle of $k[x]/(x^2)$, which is $kx\neq0$. So the first non-vanishing Ext is in degree $1$.

blocks.title: Recall: dimension of a module and systems of parameters
blocks.body:
Krull dimension and systems of parameters belong to their own page (Krull dimension and systems of parameters); here are the facts used below. Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local and $M$ finitely generated.

1. $\dim M = \dim\operatorname{Supp}M = \dim R/\operatorname{Ann}M$, the supremum of the lengths of chains of primes in $\operatorname{Supp}M$. Ficarra sets $\dim 0 = -\infty$. Since the minimal primes of $\operatorname{Supp}M$ are associated and $\operatorname{Ass}M\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}M$, $\dim M = \max\{\dim R/\mathfrak p:\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M\}$.
2. If $\mathfrak p\subsetneq\mathfrak q$ are primes then $\dim R/\mathfrak q<\dim R/\mathfrak p$, and $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p+\dim R/\mathfrak p\le\dim R$ (concatenate chains).
3. For $x\in\mathfrak m$: $\dim M/xM\ge\dim M-1$, and $\dim M/xM = \dim M-1$ if $x$ is $M$-regular (Guan-Hu Lemma 2.3; Weibel 4.4.7 for $M = R$).
4. A system of parameters of $M$ is a sequence $x_1,\dots,x_d\in\mathfrak m$, $d = \dim M$, with $M/(x_1,\dots,x_d)M$ of finite length; systems of parameters exist, and $\dim M$ is the least number of elements of $\mathfrak m$ with this property (Hochster's definition for $M = R$). Elements $x_1,\dots,x_i$ are part of a system of parameters if and only if $\dim M/(x_1,\dots,x_i)M = \dim M-i$.

blocks.title: Depth is bounded by dimension
blocks.body:
Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local and $M\neq0$ finitely generated. Then
$$\operatorname{depth}M\le\dim R/\mathfrak p\quad\text{for every }\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M.$$
Consequently $\operatorname{depth}M\le\dim M\le\dim R$, and $\operatorname{depth}M = 0$ if and only if $\mathfrak m\in\operatorname{Ass}M$, i.e. if and only if some $a\neq0$ in $M$ is killed by $\mathfrak m$. (Stacks Lemmas 10.72.3 and 10.72.9; Guan-Hu Corollary 3.13; Weibel notes $\operatorname{depth}R\le\dim R$ in 4.4.3.)

Idea: cutting by a regular element $x$ lowers the depth by exactly one; an associated prime $\mathfrak p$ of $M$ produces an associated prime of $M/xM$ that contains $\mathfrak p+(x)$, which is strictly bigger than $\mathfrak p$, so $\dim R/\mathfrak p$ drops by at least one.

Induct on $n = \operatorname{depth}M$, which is finite by the Ext theorem. For $n = 0$ there is nothing to prove. Let $n\ge1$, take an $M$-regular $x\in\mathfrak m$ and $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$, $\mathfrak p = \operatorname{Ann}(a)$. Then $x\notin\mathfrak p$, since $xa = 0$ would contradict regularity.

Put $N = \{b\in M:\mathfrak pb = 0\}$, a non-zero submodule (it contains $a$). We claim $N\cap xM = xN$. If $xm\in N$, then $x(\mathfrak pm) = \mathfrak p(xm) = 0$, so $\mathfrak pm = 0$ because $x$ is a non-zero-divisor; thus $m\in N$. Hence $N/xN = N/(N\cap xM)$ embeds in $M/xM$. Since $N$ is finitely generated and non-zero, $N/xN\neq0$ by Nakayama's lemma. Pick $b\in N$ whose class $\bar b$ in $M/xM$ is non-zero. Then $\operatorname{Ann}(\bar b)\supseteq\mathfrak p+(x)$. Every element of $\operatorname{Ann}(\bar b)$ is a zero-divisor on $M/xM$, so $\operatorname{Ann}(\bar b)\subseteq\mathfrak q$ for some $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(M/xM)$ (recalled facts). Now $\mathfrak q\supseteq\mathfrak p+(x)\supsetneq\mathfrak p$, so $\dim R/\mathfrak q\le\dim R/\mathfrak p-1$. By induction, applied to $M/xM$ of depth $n-1$,
$$n-1\le\dim R/\mathfrak q\le\dim R/\mathfrak p-1.$$

Consequences: $\dim M$ is the maximum of $\dim R/\mathfrak p$ over $\operatorname{Ass}M$, so $\operatorname{depth}M\le\dim M$, and $\dim M\le\dim R$ since $\operatorname{Supp}M\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}R$. Finally $\operatorname{depth}M = 0$ means that $\mathfrak m$ consists of zero-divisors, which by the recalled facts means $\mathfrak m\subseteq\mathfrak p$ for an associated $\mathfrak p$, i.e. $\mathfrak m\in\operatorname{Ass}M$.

items.q: What is the depth of the residue field $k$, and of any non-zero module of finite length?
items.a: $0$: for finite length $M\neq0$, $\operatorname{Supp}M = \{\mathfrak m\}$, so $\operatorname{Ass}M = \{\mathfrak m\}$; for $k$ directly, $\mathrm{Hom}(k,k)\neq0$.

items.q: What is $\operatorname{depth}$ of $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ localised at $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$?
items.a: Exactly $n$: at least $n$ because $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is regular, at most $n$ because depth is bounded by the dimension $n$.

items.q: Over $R = \mathbb Z_{(p)}$, what are the depths of $R$, $R/p^2$ and $R\oplus R/p$?
items.a: $1$, $0$ and $0$; for the sum, $\mathrm{Ext}^0(k,R\oplus R/p)\supseteq\mathrm{Hom}(k,R/p)\neq0$.

items.q: Is the depth of a module over a local ring always finite?
items.a: For $M\neq0$ yes, it is at most $\dim M$; the zero module has depth $\infty$ by convention.

blocks.title: Four ways to compute depth
blocks.body: The sources give four descriptions of the same number for a finitely generated $M\neq0$ over a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$; the first two are proved above, the last two are quoted.

items.label: Regular sequences
items.body: The length of a longest $M$-regular sequence in $\mathfrak m$: how many successive non-zero-divisors one can divide out before every element of $\mathfrak m$ becomes a zero-divisor. This is the definition; it is the description in which $\operatorname{depth}\le\dim$ and the Cohen-Macaulay property are naturally stated, and in which one computes by hand.

items.label: First non-zero Ext
items.body: The smallest $i$ with $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(k,M)\neq0$. Ext has long exact sequences, so this is the form used in proofs: the depth lemma and the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula below are read off from it. Guan and Hu's Lean formalisation takes it as the definition and proves the equality with regular sequences as a theorem (their Theorem 3.1).

items.label: Koszul homology
items.body: If $r_1,\dots,r_n$ generate an ideal $I$, then $$\operatorname{depth}_IM = n-\sup\{i: H_i(r;M)\neq0\},$$ where $H_i(r;M)$ is the homology of the Koszul complex $K(r;R)\otimes_RM$ (Iyengar-Ma-Schwede-Walker, §1.6 and Remark 1.7). The case of a regular sequence is Weibel's Corollary 4.5.4: then all $H_i$ with $i>0$ vanish. Over $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ with $I = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$ one has $H_i(x;M)\cong\mathrm{Tor}_i(k,M)$ ([[tor]]), so the depth is $n$ minus the length of a minimal resolution: this is the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula again.

items.label: Local cohomology
items.body: Weibel's Theorem 4.6.3: the depth is the smallest $q$ with $H^q_{\mathfrak m}(M)\neq0$, where $H^q_{\mathfrak m}$ are the right derived functors of $M\mapsto\{a:\mathfrak m^ja = 0\text{ for some }j\}$; by his Corollary 4.6.9, $H^q_{\mathfrak m}(M)\neq0$ only for $\operatorname{depth}M\le q\le\dim R$, and Ficarra (Proposition 1.4) quotes Grothendieck's vanishing $H^q_{\mathfrak m}(M) = 0$ for $q>\dim M$. Papers in birational geometry and mixed characteristic, such as Iyengar-Ma-Schwede-Walker, define depth this way because it extends to complexes.

blocks.title: Depth, grade and regular sequences
blocks.body: The same number appears under different names, and the edge cases are handled differently.

rows.text: Calls the length of a maximal regular sequence on $A$ in $\mathfrak m$ the grade $G(A)$ (Definition 4.4.3) and writes Auslander-Buchsbaum as $G(R) = G(A)+\mathrm{pd}(A)$; the word depth is not used.

Writes $\operatorname{depth}_I(M)$ and $\operatorname{depth}(M)$; a regular sequence must satisfy $M/(f_1,\dots,f_r)M\neq0$; $\operatorname{depth}_I(M) = \infty$ when $IM = M$, so the zero module has depth $\infty$.
$\operatorname{depth}_I(E) = \infty$ if $E/IE = 0$ or if regular sequences in $I$ have unbounded length; regular sequences require $E/(a)E\neq0$.
Distinguishes regular from possibly improper regular sequences (no condition $(x)M\neq M$); over a local ring with elements in $\mathfrak m$ they agree.
Weakly regular versus regular sequences; depth defined as the least $i$ with $\mathrm{Ext}^i(N,M)\neq0$, infinite if there is none.
Fix in their conventions that the depth of a finite module over a local ring always means the $\mathfrak m$-depth.

blocks.title: A plane meeting a line
blocks.body: Let $R$ be $k[x,y,z]/(xy,xz)$ localised at $\mathfrak m = (x,y,z)$: the plane $x = 0$ together with the line $y = z = 0$. Find $\operatorname{Ass}R$, $\dim R$ and $\operatorname{depth}R$.
blocks.solution:
Associated primes. $(xy,xz) = (x)\cap(y,z)$: the inclusion $\subseteq$ is clear, and if $xf\in(y,z)$ then $f\in(y,z)$ because $(y,z)$ is prime and $x\notin(y,z)$, so $xf\in x(y,z) = (xy,xz)$. An intersection of two primes, neither containing the other, is a primary decomposition without embedded components, so $\operatorname{Ass}R = \{(x),(y,z)\}$ (images in $R$). Directly: $(x) = \operatorname{Ann}(y)$ and $(y,z) = \operatorname{Ann}(x)$ in $R$.

Dimension. $\dim R/(x) = \dim k[y,z]_{(y,z)} = 2$ and $\dim R/(y,z) = \dim k[x]_{(x)} = 1$, so $\dim R = 2$.

Depth. The element $x+y$ lies in neither associated prime, so it is a non-zero-divisor on $R$. Modulo $x+y$, substitute $y = -x$: $R/(x+y)\cong k[x,z]/(x^2,xz)$ localised, the $z$-axis with an embedded point, in which $x\neq0$ is killed by $x$ and $z$, hence by the maximal ideal. So $\operatorname{depth}R/(x+y) = 0$, and $\operatorname{depth}R = 1$ by the theorem on dividing by a regular element.

The bound $\operatorname{depth}R\le\dim R/\mathfrak p$ is sharp here at $\mathfrak p = (y,z)$: the line is what limits the depth.

blocks.body:
- Depth depends on the ideal. For $R = k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ and $I = (x)$, $\operatorname{depth}_IR = 1$ while $\operatorname{depth}R = 2$. When a paper says "depth" for a module over a local ring it means the $\mathfrak m$-depth, as Holanda and Miranda-Neto state explicitly.
- Depth $0$ does not mean finite length: $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}/(x^2,xy)$ has depth $0$ and dimension $1$. It means only that $\mathfrak m$ is an associated prime.
- Depth is not monotone along submodules: $\mathfrak m\subset R = k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ has depth $1$ while $R$ has depth $2$, and $k = R/\mathfrak m$ has depth $0$ (see the depth lemma below).
- A sequence that is regular in some order need not be regular in another order outside the local or graded case (Section 1).

items.q: Compute the depth of the $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$-modules $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $\mathbb Z_{(p)}/p^n$ ($n\ge1$) and $\mathbb Z_{(p)}\oplus\mathbb Z/p$.
items.hint: Look for an element killed by the maximal ideal $(p)$.
items.solution: $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$: $p$ is regular and $\mathbb Z_{(p)}/p = \mathbb F_p$ has depth $0$, so the depth is $1$. $\mathbb Z_{(p)}/p^n$: the class of $p^{n-1}$ is non-zero and killed by $p$, so the depth is $0$. The direct sum contains $(0,1)$, non-zero and killed by $p$, so its depth is $0$.

items.q: Show that $\operatorname{depth}(M\oplus N) = \min\{\operatorname{depth}M,\operatorname{depth}N\}$ for non-zero finitely generated $M,N$ over a local ring.
items.hint: $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,-)$ commutes with finite direct sums.
items.solution: $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M\oplus N)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)\oplus\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N)$, which vanishes exactly when both summands vanish. So the first non-vanishing index for $M\oplus N$ is the smaller of the two first non-vanishing indices.

items.q: Prove the Koszul formula $\operatorname{depth}_IM = n-\sup\{i:H_i(r;M)\neq0\}$ in the case $n = 1$, $I = (r)$, $IM\neq M$.
items.hint: The Koszul complex on one element is $0\to M\xrightarrow{r}M\to0$ in degrees $1,0$.
items.solution:
$H_1(r;M) = \{a: ra = 0\}$ and $H_0(r;M) = M/rM
eq0$. If $r$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M$, then $H_1 = 0$, the supremum is $0$, and the formula gives $1$; indeed $r$ is $M$-regular, and it cannot be extended inside $(r)$, because every element $sr$ of $I$ acts as $0$ on $M/rM
eq0$; so $\operatorname{depth}_IM = 1$. If $r$ is a zero-divisor, $H_1
eq0$, the formula gives $0$, and indeed every element $sr$ of $I$ kills any $a
eq0$ with $ra = 0$, so no element of $I$ is regular.

items.q: Let $R = k[x,y]$ localised at $(x,y)$ and $M = R/(x^2,xy)$. Show that $\operatorname{Ass}M = \{(x),(x,y)\}$, and use the theorem on depth and dimension to explain why the embedded prime forces $\operatorname{depth}M = 0$.
items.hint: $\operatorname{Ann}(\bar x)$ and $\operatorname{Ann}(\bar y)$.
items.solution: $\operatorname{Ann}(\bar x) = (x,y)$, since $x\cdot x$ and $y\cdot x$ lie in $(x^2,xy)$ but $1\cdot x$ does not. $\operatorname{Ann}(\bar y) = (x)$: $xy\in(x^2,xy)$, and if $fy\in(x^2,xy)\subseteq(x)$ then $f\in(x)$. So both primes are associated. Every associated prime contains $\operatorname{Ann}M = (x^2,xy)$, hence $x$, so it is $(x)$ or a prime containing $(x)$ properly; in the local ring $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ the primes containing $x$ are $(x)$ and those $(x,f)$ with $f\in k[y]$ irreducible vanishing at $0$, i.e. $(x,y)$. So $\operatorname{Ass}M = \{(x),(x,y)\}$. The theorem gives $\operatorname{depth}M\le\dim R/(x,y) = 0$: the embedded point bounds the depth, although $\dim M = \dim R/(x) = 1$.

items.q: Let $M\neq0$ over a local ring have depth $n$, and let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be any maximal $M$-regular sequence in $\mathfrak m$. Show that $\mathrm{Ext}^n(k,M)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(k,M/(x_1,\dots,x_n)M)$. Deduce that the dimension of the socle $\{a:\mathfrak ma = 0\}$ of $M/(x_1,\dots,x_n)M$ does not depend on the choice of the sequence.
items.hint: Apply the isomorphism $\mathrm{Ext}^n(k,M)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{n-1}(k,M/x_1M)$ repeatedly.
items.solution: Write $M_i = M/(x_1,\dots,x_i)M$. Each $x_{i+1}$ is $M_i$-regular and $\operatorname{depth}M_i = n-i$ (depth drops by one at each step). The isomorphism of the theorem on dividing by a regular element, applied to $M_i$ and $x_{i+1}$, gives $\mathrm{Ext}^{n-i}(k,M_i)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{n-i-1}(k,M_{i+1})$. Chaining these for $i = 0,\dots,n-1$: $\mathrm{Ext}^n(k,M)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^0(k,M_n) = \mathrm{Hom}(k,M_n)$. A homomorphism $k\to M_n$ is determined by the image of $1$, an element killed by $\mathfrak m$; so $\mathrm{Hom}(k,M_n)$ is the socle of $M_n$, a $k$-vector space. Its dimension equals $\dim_k\mathrm{Ext}^n(k,M)$, which involves no choice. (This number is the type of $M$; it reappears in the Gorenstein section.)

blocks.body:
- $\operatorname{depth}_IM$ is the common length of all non-extendable $M$-regular sequences in $I$, and equals $\min\{i:\mathrm{Ext}^i(R/I,M)\neq0\}$.
- Dividing by a regular element lowers depth by exactly one.
- $\operatorname{depth}M\le\dim R/\mathfrak p$ for every associated prime, so $\operatorname{depth}M\le\dim M\le\dim R$; depth $0$ means $\mathfrak m$ is associated.
- Equivalent descriptions: Koszul homology ($n$ minus the top non-vanishing index) and local cohomology (first non-vanishing $H^i_{\mathfrak m}$).
- Embedded or lower-dimensional associated primes limit the depth.

blocks.title: The depth lemma and the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to propagate depth along short exact sequences and to read the depth of a module off a minimal free resolution.

Computing Ext by hand is laborious. In practice the depth of a module over a polynomial or regular local ring is read off from the length of its minimal free resolution, which computer algebra produces directly. Why should the length of a resolution, a homological quantity, know how many regular elements there are? The bridge is the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula $\mathrm{pd}M+\operatorname{depth}M = \operatorname{depth}R$, proved here from the Ext description of depth. Throughout, $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ is Noetherian local and modules are finitely generated; $\mathrm{pd}$ and minimal resolutions are as in [[ext]] (section on homological dimension).

blocks.title: Depth lemma

blocks.body:
Apply $\mathrm{Hom}(k,-)$ and use the Ext description of depth. The long exact sequence contains the segments
$$\begin{gathered}\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N')\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N''),\\ \mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N'')\to\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,N'),\\ \mathrm{Ext}^{i-1}(k,N'')\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N')\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N),\end{gathered}$$
with $\mathrm{Ext}^{-1} = 0$. In each, if both outer terms vanish so does the middle one. For 1, take $i<\min\{\operatorname{depth}N',\operatorname{depth}N''\}$ in the first segment. For 2, take $i<\min\{\operatorname{depth}N,\operatorname{depth}N'-1\}$ in the second: then $i<\operatorname{depth}N$ and $i+1<\operatorname{depth}N'$. For 3, take $i<\min\{\operatorname{depth}N,\operatorname{depth}N''+1\}$ in the third: then $i-1<\operatorname{depth}N''$ and $i<\operatorname{depth}N$. In each case all $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,-)$ of the module in question vanish below the stated bound, which is the claim.

blocks.title: The depth of the maximal ideal
blocks.body: Let $R = k[x,y]$ localised at $\mathfrak m = (x,y)$. Use the depth lemma on $0\to\mathfrak m\to R\to k\to0$ to find $\operatorname{depth}\mathfrak m$.
blocks.solution: We know $\operatorname{depth}R = 2$ and $\operatorname{depth}k = 0$. Part 3: $\operatorname{depth}\mathfrak m\ge\min\{\operatorname{depth}R,\operatorname{depth}k+1\} = \min\{2,1\} = 1$. Part 2: $\operatorname{depth}k\ge\min\{\operatorname{depth}R,\operatorname{depth}\mathfrak m-1\}$, i.e. $0\ge\min\{2,\operatorname{depth}\mathfrak m-1\}$, which forces $\operatorname{depth}\mathfrak m\le1$. So $\operatorname{depth}\mathfrak m = 1$. Directly: $x$ is regular on $\mathfrak m$ (a submodule of a domain), and in $\mathfrak m/x\mathfrak m$ the class of $x$ is non-zero (since $x\notin x\mathfrak m$) and killed by $x$ and by $y$ (as $yx = xy\in x\mathfrak m$), so $x$ cannot be extended.

blocks.title: Auslander-Buchsbaum formula
blocks.body:
Let $M\neq0$ be a finitely generated $R$-module of finite projective dimension. Then
$$\mathrm{pd}_RM+\operatorname{depth}M = \operatorname{depth}R.$$
(Stacks Proposition 10.111.1; Weibel Theorem 4.4.15; Guan-Hu Theorem 3.8.) In particular $\mathrm{pd}_RM\le\operatorname{depth}R$.

The sources argue by induction in different ways. The Stacks Project inducts on $\operatorname{depth}M$: when it is positive it divides out an element regular on both $R$ and $M$, and when $\operatorname{depth}M = 0$ it splits a minimal free resolution into short exact sequences and applies the depth lemma. Weibel uses a double induction with his change-of-rings theorems. Guan and Hu treat projective dimension $1$ as the core case and then induct on $\mathrm{pd}M$, which is the arrangement followed here; it uses only the Ext description of depth and the fact that a minimal resolution has differentials with entries in $\mathfrak m$.

Write $d = \operatorname{depth}R$ and $n = \mathrm{pd}M$. Take a minimal free resolution $0\to F_n\to\cdots\to F_0\to M\to0$ ([[ext]], minimal resolutions over local rings): $F_i\cong R^{\beta_i}$, $F_n\neq0$, and every differential has matrix entries in $\mathfrak m$. Two remarks. Since $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,-)$ is additive, $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,R^b)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,R)^b$, which for $b\ge1$ vanishes for $i<d$ and not for $i = d$. And a map $\varphi\colon R^b\to R^c$ whose matrix has entries in $\mathfrak m$ induces zero on each $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,-)$: the induced map is the matrix of the maps induced by multiplication by the entries, which vanish by observation (b) in the proof of the Ext theorem.

Case $n = 0$. $M\cong R^{\beta_0}$ with $\beta_0\ge1$, so $\operatorname{depth}M = d$.

Case $n = 1$. The resolution is $0\to F_1\xrightarrow{\varphi}F_0\to M\to0$, $F_1\neq0$. All maps induced by $\varphi$ vanish, so the long exact Ext sequence breaks into short exact sequences
$$0\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,F_0)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)\to\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,F_1)\to0\quad(i\ge0),$$
and moreover $\mathrm{Hom}(k,F_1) = 0$, because $\mathrm{Hom}(k,F_1)\to\mathrm{Hom}(k,F_0)$ is injective (left exactness) and zero. Since $F_1\neq0$, this forces $d\ge1$. Now $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M) = 0$ exactly when $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,R)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,R)$ both vanish, that is, when $i+1<d$. Hence $\operatorname{depth}M = d-1$.

Case $n\ge2$. Let $K = \operatorname{im}(F_1\to F_0)$. Then $K\neq0$ (else $M\cong F_0$ would be free), $0\to K\to F_0\to M\to0$ is exact, and $0\to F_n\to\cdots\to F_1\to K\to0$ is a minimal free resolution, so $\mathrm{pd}K = n-1$ (the length of a minimal resolution is the projective dimension, by the Tor criterion of [[ext]]). By induction $\operatorname{depth}K = d-n+1$, so $d\ge n-1\ge1$. In the exact segment
$$\begin{aligned}&\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,F_0)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)\\ &\quad\to\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,K)\to\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,F_0)\end{aligned}$$
the outer terms vanish when $i+1<d$, so $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,K)$ for $0\le i\le d-2$. The case $d = n-1$ is impossible: it would give $\operatorname{depth}K = 0$, so $\mathrm{Hom}(k,K)\neq0$, whereas $\mathrm{Hom}(k,K)$ embeds in $\mathrm{Hom}(k,F_0) = 0$ (as $d\ge1$). So $d\ge n$, hence $d-n\le d-2$, and the isomorphism gives $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M) = 0$ for $i<d-n$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^{d-n}(k,M)\neq0$. So $\operatorname{depth}M = d-n$.

blocks.title: Recall: regular local rings
blocks.body: Regular local rings have their own page (regular local rings and the Auslander-Buchsbaum-Serre theorem); here is what this page uses. A Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m)$ is regular if $\mathfrak m$ can be generated by $\dim R$ elements (the minimal number of generators is always at least $\dim R$). Examples: fields, $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ localised at $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, $k[\![x_1,\dots,x_n]\!]$. Facts quoted without proof: a regular local ring is a domain (Guan-Hu Theorem 5.3); and $R$ is regular if and only if every finitely generated module has finite projective dimension, in which case $\mathrm{pd}M\le\dim R$ (Auslander-Buchsbaum-Serre: Weibel Theorem 4.4.16, Guan-Hu Theorem 5.16).

blocks.title: Depth from a resolution
blocks.body:
Let $S$ be a regular local ring of dimension $n$ and $M\neq0$ a finitely generated $S$-module. Then
$$\operatorname{depth}M = n-\mathrm{pd}_SM.$$
The same formula holds for finitely generated graded modules over $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, with depth taken at $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ and $\mathrm{pd}$ the length of a minimal graded free resolution. If $M = S/I$ is a quotient ring, its depth as a ring equals its depth as an $S$-module, since the elements of $\mathfrak m_S$ act through their images in $\mathfrak m_{S/I}$, which they cover.

$\mathrm{pd}_SM<\infty$ by Auslander-Buchsbaum-Serre, and $\operatorname{depth}S = n$ because $S$ is Cohen-Macaulay (proved in the next section; directly, a minimal generating set of $\mathfrak m$ is a regular sequence of length $n = \dim S$). Now apply the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula. For the graded statement, localise at $\mathfrak m = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$: a minimal graded free resolution of $M$ becomes a free resolution of $M_{\mathfrak m}$ whose matrices still have entries in $\mathfrak m$, hence a minimal one, so its length is $\mathrm{pd}M_{\mathfrak m}$; and the depth at the origin is by definition that of $M_{\mathfrak m}$. The last sentence: a sequence in $\mathfrak m_S$ is $M$-regular exactly when its image in $S/I$ is, because both conditions only involve the action on $M$.

items.q: Over $R = k[x,y,z]_{(x,y,z)}$, a module has a minimal free resolution of length $2$. What is its depth?
Can a module of finite projective dimension over a ring of depth $2$ have projective dimension $3$?
items.a: No: $\mathrm{pd}M = \operatorname{depth}R-\operatorname{depth}M\le2$.

items.q: In $0\to N'\to N\to N''\to0$, $\operatorname{depth}N' = 3$ and $\operatorname{depth}N'' = 1$. What does the depth lemma say about $\operatorname{depth}N$?
items.a: $\operatorname{depth}N\ge\min\{3,1\} = 1$; and part 2 gives $1\ge\min\{\operatorname{depth}N,2\}$, so $\operatorname{depth}N = 1$.

blocks.title: Checking Auslander-Buchsbaum over k[x,y]
blocks.body: Let $R = k[x,y]$ localised at $\mathfrak m = (x,y)$. Compute depth and projective dimension of $R$, $R/(x)$, $k$ and $M = R/(x^2,xy)$, and check the formula.
blocks.solution:
Depth via Ext: the Koszul complex $0\to R\to R^2\to R\to k\to0$ of [[tor]] is a free resolution of $k$, so $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N)$ is the cohomology of $N\to N^2\to N$, $n\mapsto(xn,yn)$, $(a,b)\mapsto-ya+xb$. Its $H^0$ is the socle $\{n:\mathfrak mn = 0\}$ and its $H^2$ is $N/\mathfrak mN$.

1. $R$: free, $\mathrm{pd} = 0$; $x,y$ is regular and $R/(x,y) = k$ has depth $0$, so $\operatorname{depth}R = 2$. Formula: $0+2 = 2$.
2. $R/(x)$: resolution $0\to R\xrightarrow{x}R\to R/(x)\to0$, so $\mathrm{pd} = 1$ (it is not free, being killed by $x$). In the cochain complex for $N = R/(x)$, a localisation of $k[y]$, the socle is $0$ and $H^1 = \{(0,b)\}/\{(0,yn)\}\cong k\neq0$, so the depth is $1$. Formula: $1+1 = 2$.
3. $k$: the Koszul resolution has length $2$ and is minimal, so $\mathrm{pd}k = 2$; the socle of $k$ is $k$, so the depth is $0$. Formula: $2+0 = 2$.
4. $M = R/(x^2,xy)$. The map $(a,b)\mapsto x^2a+xyb = x(xa+yb)$ has kernel $\{(a,b): xa+yb = 0\} = R\cdot(y,-x)$, since $x$ and $y$ are coprime in the factorial domain $R$. So
$$0\to R\xrightarrow{\binom{y}{-x}}R^2\xrightarrow{(x^2\ \ xy)}R\to M\to0$$
is a minimal free resolution and $\mathrm{pd}M = 2$. The class of $x$ is a non-zero socle element, so $\operatorname{depth}M = 0$. Formula: $2+0 = 2$. Note that $M$ is not of finite length (the powers of $y$ survive): depth $0$ does not require finite length.

blocks.title: Two non-Cohen-Macaulay rings through resolutions
blocks.body: Use resolutions to compute the depth of (a) $A = S/(xy,xz)$ with $S = k[x,y,z]$, the plane and the line of the previous section, and (b) $B = T/I$ with $T = k[w,x,y,z]$ and $I = (wy,wz,xy,xz)$, two planes meeting in a point. Depth is taken at the origin.
blocks.solution:
(a) As in the previous example, $(a,b)\mapsto x(ya+zb)$ has kernel $S\cdot(z,-y)$ because $y,z$ are coprime. So $0\to S\to S^2\to S\to A\to0$ is a minimal resolution, $\mathrm{pd}_SA = 2$ and $\operatorname{depth}A = 3-2 = 1$, matching the direct computation.

(b) $I = (w,x)(y,z) = (w,x)\cap(y,z)$, and its minimal resolution has the shape
$$0\to T\to T^4\to T^4\to T\to B\to0,$$
with Betti numbers $1,4,4,1$; one way to obtain them is to compute the Koszul homology $H_i(w,x,y,z;B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}_i(k,B)$ degree by degree, which the checks of this page do. So $\mathrm{pd}_TB = 3$ and $\operatorname{depth}B = 4-3 = 1$. A regular element can be seen directly: $w+y$ lies in neither associated prime $(w,x)$, $(y,z)$, so it is a non-zero-divisor; modulo $w+y$ (substitute $y = -w$) the ideal becomes $(w^2,wz,wx,xz)$, and the class of $w$ is killed by $w,x,z$ (and by $y = -w$), so it is a socle element and the depth of $B/(w+y)$ is $0$. Both rings have dimension $2$, so neither is Cohen-Macaulay.

blocks.body:
- The formula needs $\mathrm{pd}M<\infty$. Over $R = k[x]/(x^2)$, the residue field has the infinite resolution $\cdots\xrightarrow{x}R\xrightarrow{x}R\to k\to0$; both $k$ and $R$ have depth $0$, and no formula relates them.
- It is $\operatorname{depth}R$, not $\dim R$, that appears; the two agree when $R$ is Cohen-Macaulay, which is how the formula is usually quoted over regular rings.
- In the depth lemma the inequalities can be strict in either direction; only the minimum is controlled. For instance $0\to R\xrightarrow{x}R\to R/(x)\to0$ over $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ has depths $2,2,1$.

items.q: Let $R = k[x,y,z]$ localised at $(x,y,z)$ and $M = R/(x,y)$. Compute $\mathrm{pd}M$ and $\operatorname{depth}M$ and check Auslander-Buchsbaum.
items.hint: $x,y$ is a regular sequence, so its Koszul complex resolves $R/(x,y)$.
items.solution: The Koszul complex $0\to R\to R^2\to R\to R/(x,y)\to0$ is a free resolution with entries in $\mathfrak m$, hence minimal, so $\mathrm{pd}M = 2$. $M\cong k[z]_{(z)}$; $z$ is $M$-regular and $M/zM = k$ has depth $0$, so $\operatorname{depth}M = 1$. Formula: $2+1 = 3 = \operatorname{depth}R$.

items.q: Let $0\to K\to F\to M\to0$ be exact with $F\neq0$ free and $\operatorname{depth}M<\operatorname{depth}R$. Use the depth lemma to show $\operatorname{depth}K = \operatorname{depth}M+1$.
items.hint: Apply parts 2 and 3 with $\operatorname{depth}F = \operatorname{depth}R$.
items.solution: $K\neq0$: otherwise $M\cong F$ would have depth $\operatorname{depth}R$. (If $M = 0$ the hypothesis $\operatorname{depth}M = \infty<\operatorname{depth}R$ fails, so $M\neq0$.) Part 3: $$\operatorname{depth}K\ge\min\{\operatorname{depth}F,\operatorname{depth}M+1\} = \operatorname{depth}M+1,$$ because $\operatorname{depth}M+1\le\operatorname{depth}R = \operatorname{depth}F$. Part 2: $\operatorname{depth}M\ge\min\{\operatorname{depth}F,\operatorname{depth}K-1\}$; since $\operatorname{depth}M<\operatorname{depth}F$, the minimum must be $\operatorname{depth}K-1$, so $\operatorname{depth}K\le\operatorname{depth}M+1$.

items.q: Suppose $\operatorname{depth}R = 0$. Show, both from Auslander-Buchsbaum and directly from a minimal resolution and a non-zero socle element $s$ of $R$, that every finitely generated module of finite projective dimension is free.
items.hint: For the direct proof, look at the last map $F_n\to F_{n-1}$ of a minimal resolution and apply it to $s e$ for a basis vector $e$.
items.solution: From the formula: $\mathrm{pd}M = 0-\operatorname{depth}M\le0$, so $M$ is projective, hence free over the local ring. Directly: suppose $n = \mathrm{pd}M\ge1$ and take a minimal resolution with last map $\varphi\colon F_n\to F_{n-1}$, injective, with entries in $\mathfrak m$. For a basis vector $e$ of $F_n\neq0$, $\varphi(se) = s\varphi(e)$, and every coordinate of $\varphi(e)$ lies in $\mathfrak m$, which kills $s$. So $\varphi(se) = 0$ with $se\neq0$, contradicting injectivity. Hence $n = 0$.

items.q: Let $R = k[x,y]$ localised at $(x,y)$ and $M = R/(x^2,xy,y^2)$. Without computing a resolution, find $\mathrm{pd}M$; then verify it with an explicit resolution.
items.hint: $M$ has finite length. For the resolution, the relations among $x^2,xy,y^2$ are generated by two syzygies.
items.solution: $M$ has finite length and is non-zero, so $\operatorname{depth}M = 0$ and Auslander-Buchsbaum gives $\mathrm{pd}M = 2-0 = 2$. Explicitly, $0\to R^2\xrightarrow{\psi}R^3\xrightarrow{(x^2\ xy\ y^2)}R\to M\to0$ with $\psi$ the matrix with columns $(y,-x,0)^T$ and $(0,y,-x)^T$: these are relations ($x^2y-xyx = 0$, $xy\cdot y-y^2x = 0$), $\psi$ is injective (its $2\times2$ minors $y^2,-xy,x^2$ have no common factor) and the kernel of $(x^2\ xy\ y^2)$ is generated by the two columns (Hilbert-Burch; the checks confirm exactness degree by degree). Length $2$, as predicted.

items.q: Let $R$ be local with $\operatorname{depth}R = d$ and $M\neq0$ of finite projective dimension. Show that for $0\le j\le\mathrm{pd}M$ the $j$-th syzygy $\Omega_j$ of $M$ in a minimal free resolution satisfies $\operatorname{depth}\Omega_j = \operatorname{depth}M+j$, and that $\Omega_j$ is free only for $j = \mathrm{pd}M$.
items.hint: Induct on $j$ with the standard exercise above; or apply Auslander-Buchsbaum to $\Omega_j$, whose minimal resolution is a truncation of that of $M$.
items.solution: Let $p = \mathrm{pd}M$. The truncated resolution $0\to F_p\to\cdots\to F_j\to\Omega_j\to0$ is a minimal free resolution of $\Omega_j = \operatorname{im}(F_j\to F_{j-1})$ (with $\Omega_0 = M$), of length $p-j$ with $F_p\neq0$, so $\mathrm{pd}\,\Omega_j = p-j$ and $\Omega_j\neq0$. Auslander-Buchsbaum: $\operatorname{depth}\Omega_j = d-(p-j)$, which is $(d-p)+j = \operatorname{depth}M+j$. $\Omega_j$ is free if and only if $\mathrm{pd}\,\Omega_j = 0$, i.e. $j = p$. In particular, if $R$ is Cohen-Macaulay ($d = \dim R$), $\Omega_j$ is maximal Cohen-Macaulay only for $j = p$, where it is free.

blocks.body:
- Depth lemma: along $0\to N'\to N\to N''\to0$, $\operatorname{depth}N\ge\min(\operatorname{depth}N',\operatorname{depth}N'')$ and two shifted variants; all three come from the long exact Ext sequence.
- Auslander-Buchsbaum: $\mathrm{pd}M+\operatorname{depth}M = \operatorname{depth}R$ when $\mathrm{pd}M<\infty$.
- Over a regular local or polynomial ring $S$ of dimension $n$: $\operatorname{depth}M = n-\mathrm{pd}_SM$, the practical way to compute depth.
- Example: two planes meeting in a point have Betti numbers $1,4,4,1$, so depth $1<2 = \dim$.

blocks.title: Cohen-Macaulay modules and rings
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to decide whether a local ring or module is Cohen-Macaulay, by exhibiting a system of parameters that is a regular sequence, by computing depth, by recognising an obstruction (an embedded prime or components of different dimension), or by checking freeness over a polynomial subring.

Depth never exceeds dimension. Ji describes depth as a variant of dimension that measures "from big to small", by successive cuts, while dimension measures chains of primes; Cohen-Macaulay means the two counts agree. The three rings met so far that fail this are pictured below. Each failure has a geometric reason: an embedded point, components of different dimensions, or two components that meet in too small a set.

blocks.caption: Three rings that are not Cohen-Macaulay at the origin: (a) $k[x,y]/(x^2,xy)$, a line with an embedded point (depth $0$, dimension $1$); (b) $k[x,y,z]/(xy,xz)$, a plane and a line (depth $1$, dimension $2$); (c) $k[w,x,y,z]/((w,x)\cap(y,z))$, two planes meeting in one point (depth $1$, dimension $2$).
blocks.alt: Three sketches side by side. Left: a vertical line with a small shaded disc around a point on it, labelled a. Middle: a shaded parallelogram (a plane) pierced by a vertical line, labelled b. Right: two shaded parallelograms touching at a single corner point, labelled c.

blocks.title: Cohen-Macaulay and maximal Cohen-Macaulay
blocks.body:
Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring and $M$ a finitely generated $R$-module.

1. $M$ is Cohen-Macaulay if $M = 0$ or $\operatorname{depth}M = \dim M$ (recall $\dim M = \dim\operatorname{Supp}M$).
2. $R$ is a Cohen-Macaulay ring if it is Cohen-Macaulay as a module over itself: $\operatorname{depth}R = \dim R$.
3. $M$ is maximal Cohen-Macaulay (MCM) if $\operatorname{depth}M = \dim R$. For $M\neq0$ this means: $M$ is Cohen-Macaulay and $\dim M = \dim R$, because $\operatorname{depth}M\le\dim M\le\dim R$.

For a Noetherian ring $R$ that is not local, a finitely generated $M$ is Cohen-Macaulay if $M_{\mathfrak m}$ is Cohen-Macaulay over $R_{\mathfrak m}$ for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$; by the localisation theorem below, this is the same as asking it for every prime. A scheme is Cohen-Macaulay if all its local rings are.

blocks.title: Cohen-Macaulay: edge cases and global versions

rows.text: $M$ is Cohen-Macaulay if $\dim\operatorname{Supp}(M) = \operatorname{depth}(M)$ (Definition 10.103.1); maximal Cohen-Macaulay if $\operatorname{depth}M = \dim R$ (10.103.8); globally, $M_{\mathfrak p}$ Cohen-Macaulay for every prime $\mathfrak p$ (10.103.12); a ring is Cohen-Macaulay if all its local rings are (10.104.6).
Global definition via localisations at maximal ideals; the zero module counts as Cohen-Macaulay by convention; maximal Cohen-Macaulay globally means maximal Cohen-Macaulay at every maximal ideal.

$M$ is Cohen-Macaulay if $M = 0$ or $\operatorname{depth}M = \dim M$ (Definition 4.1); a ring is Cohen-Macaulay if $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is for every prime (Definition 4.11), and Lemma 4.12 shows maximal ideals suffice.
Defines a local ring to be Cohen-Macaulay if some, equivalently every, system of parameters is a regular sequence.
Depth equal to dimension for local rings; a ring is Cohen-Macaulay if its localisations at all maximal ideals are (Definition 1.13).
Maximal Cohen-Macaulay is a property of complexes too: a big Cohen-Macaulay complex with finitely generated homology; a big Cohen-Macaulay module need not be finitely generated.

items.q: Is every Artinian local ring Cohen-Macaulay?
items.a: Yes: its dimension is $0$, and $0\le\operatorname{depth}\le\dim = 0$.

items.q: Over a Cohen-Macaulay local ring $R$, is $R^n$ maximal Cohen-Macaulay? Is $k$?
items.a: $R^n$ is, since $\operatorname{depth}R^n = \operatorname{depth}R = \dim R$. $k$ is Cohen-Macaulay (dimension $0$) but maximal Cohen-Macaulay only if $\dim R = 0$.

items.q: Is $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}/(x^2,xy)$ Cohen-Macaulay?
items.a: No: its depth is $0$ (the class of $x$ is killed by $\mathfrak m$) and its dimension is $1$.

blocks.title: First properties of Cohen-Macaulay modules
blocks.body:
Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local and $M\neq0$ a finitely generated Cohen-Macaulay module of dimension $d$.

1. Every $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$ satisfies $\dim R/\mathfrak p = d$. In particular every associated prime is minimal in $\operatorname{Supp}M$: $M$ has no embedded primes.
2. For $x\in\mathfrak m$ the following are equivalent: $x$ is $M$-regular; $x$ lies in no associated prime of $M$; $\dim M/xM = d-1$. In that case $M/xM$ is Cohen-Macaulay of dimension $d-1$.
3. Conversely, for any finitely generated $M$ and $M$-regular $x\in\mathfrak m$: if $M/xM$ is Cohen-Macaulay, so is $M$.
4. For $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\mathfrak m$ the following are equivalent: $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is $M$-regular; $\dim M/(x_1,\dots,x_n)M = d-n$; $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is part of a system of parameters of $M$. In particular every system of parameters of $M$ is $M$-regular.
5. If some system of parameters of a module $N\neq0$ is $N$-regular, then $N$ is Cohen-Macaulay.

(Stacks Lemmas 10.103.3, 10.103.5, 10.103.7 and Proposition 10.103.4; Guan-Hu Lemmas 4.2-4.4; Hochster's definition is parts 4-5.)

1. For $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$: $d = \operatorname{depth}M\le\dim R/\mathfrak p\le\dim M = d$, by the theorem bounding depth and because $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Supp}M$. So $\dim R/\mathfrak p = d$. If $\mathfrak p$ were not minimal in $\operatorname{Supp}M$, some $\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak p$ would lie in $\operatorname{Supp}M$, and $\dim R/\mathfrak q>\dim R/\mathfrak p = d = \dim M$, which is impossible.

2. A regular element lies in no associated prime (associated primes consist of zero-divisors), and conversely an element outside all associated primes is a non-zero-divisor; condition 2 of regularity is Nakayama. If $x$ is regular, then $\dim M/xM = d-1$ by the recalled dimension fact. Conversely, suppose $\dim M/xM = d-1$ but $x\in\mathfrak p$ for some $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$. Then $\mathfrak p\supseteq\operatorname{Ann}M+(x)$, so $\mathfrak p\in V(\operatorname{Ann}M+(x)) = \operatorname{Supp}(M/xM)$, giving $\dim M/xM\ge\dim R/\mathfrak p = d$ by part 1, a contradiction. Finally, if $x$ is regular, $\operatorname{depth}M/xM = d-1$ (depth drops by one) and $\dim M/xM = d-1$, so $M/xM$ is Cohen-Macaulay.

3. $$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{depth}M &= \operatorname{depth}M/xM+1\\ &= \dim M/xM+1 = \dim M,\end{aligned}$$ using that depth drops by exactly one and dimension drops by exactly one for a regular element. ($M/xM\neq0$ by Nakayama, so its depth is finite.)

4. If the sequence is regular, part 2 applied successively to $M, M/x_1M,\dots$ (each Cohen-Macaulay by the previous step) shows $\dim M/(x_1,\dots,x_i)M = d-i$ for all $i$. Conversely, if $\dim M/(x_1,\dots,x_n)M = d-n$, then since each $x_i$ lowers the dimension by at most one, it lowers it by exactly one at every step; by induction, $M/(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1})M$ is Cohen-Macaulay of dimension $d-i+1$ and $x_i$ lowers its dimension by one, so part 2 shows $x_i$ is regular on it. The equivalence with "part of a system of parameters" is the recalled fact on systems of parameters. A full system of parameters has $\dim M/(x)M = 0 = d-d$.

5. A regular system of parameters has length $\dim N$, so $\operatorname{depth}N\ge\dim N$, and the reverse inequality always holds.

blocks.title: Localisation preserves the Cohen-Macaulay property
blocks.body: Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local and $M$ a finitely generated Cohen-Macaulay module. Then $M_{\mathfrak p}$ is a Cohen-Macaulay $R_{\mathfrak p}$-module for every prime $\mathfrak p$. Consequently, for a Noetherian ring, asking $M_{\mathfrak m}$ to be Cohen-Macaulay for all maximal ideals is the same as asking $M_{\mathfrak p}$ to be Cohen-Macaulay for all primes. (Stacks Lemma 10.103.11; Guan-Hu Lemma 4.5 and Lemma 4.12.)

Idea: induct on $\operatorname{depth}M_{\mathfrak p}$; when it is positive, $\mathfrak p$ avoids all associated primes of $M$ (they are minimal), so $\mathfrak p$ contains an $M$-regular element, and both depth and dimension of $M_{\mathfrak p}$ drop by one modulo it.

If $\mathfrak p\notin\operatorname{Supp}M$, then $M_{\mathfrak p} = 0$, which is Cohen-Macaulay by convention. Let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Supp}M$ and induct on $t = \operatorname{depth}M_{\mathfrak p}$, which is finite.

$t = 0$: then $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}\in\operatorname{Ass}M_{\mathfrak p}$, so $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$ (fact 4 on associated primes). By part 1 of the previous theorem $\mathfrak p$ is minimal in $\operatorname{Supp}M$, so $\operatorname{Supp}M_{\mathfrak p} = \{\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}\}$ and $\dim M_{\mathfrak p} = 0 = t$.

$t\ge1$: then $\mathfrak p\notin\operatorname{Ass}M$. Moreover $\mathfrak p$ is contained in no $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}M$: such a $\mathfrak q$ is minimal in $\operatorname{Supp}M$ (part 1) and $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Supp}M$, so $\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak q$ would give $\mathfrak p = \mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}M$. As $\operatorname{Ass}M$ is finite, prime avoidance gives $x\in\mathfrak p$ outside every associated prime, so $x$ is $M$-regular, and $x\in\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak m$. By part 2, $M/xM$ is Cohen-Macaulay. By the localisation theorem for regular sequences, $x/1$ is $M_{\mathfrak p}$-regular, so $(M/xM)_{\mathfrak p} = M_{\mathfrak p}/xM_{\mathfrak p}$ has depth $t-1$ and dimension $\dim M_{\mathfrak p}-1$. By induction it is Cohen-Macaulay: $\dim M_{\mathfrak p}-1 = t-1$. Hence $\dim M_{\mathfrak p} = \operatorname{depth}M_{\mathfrak p}$.

For the last sentence: every prime lies in a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and $M_{\mathfrak p} = (M_{\mathfrak m})_{\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak m}}$.

blocks.title: Further stability properties (quoted)
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be a Noetherian Cohen-Macaulay ring.

1. If $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is a regular sequence in a local Cohen-Macaulay ring, then $R/(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is Cohen-Macaulay (part 4 above).
2. $R[x]$ is Cohen-Macaulay, hence so is $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ (Stacks Lemma 10.104.7, Ji Proposition 2.1, Guan-Hu §4.2); so is $R[\![x]\!]$ (Wikipedia).
3. A Noetherian local ring is Cohen-Macaulay if and only if its completion is (Wikipedia).
4. Cohen-Macaulay rings are universally catenary (Ji Proposition 2.6; Hochster). The local statement behind this is proved in the next section.

Proofs of 2-4: see [stacks-cm] Lemmas 10.103.13 and 10.104.7, and [hochster615], sections on catenary rings and on flat extensions.

blocks.title: Which local rings are Cohen-Macaulay?
blocks.body: Show that the following local rings are Cohen-Macaulay: (a) Artinian local rings, such as $k[x]/(x^2)$; (b) regular local rings; (c) reduced local rings of dimension $1$, such as the node $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}/(xy)$ and the cusp $k[t^2,t^3]$ localised at $(t^2,t^3)$; (d) quotients $S/(f_1,\dots,f_c)$ of a regular local ring $S$ by a regular sequence, such as $k[x,y,z]_{(x,y,z)}/(x^2,yz)$.
blocks.solution:
(a) Dimension $0$ forces depth $0$ = dimension. Note that $k[x]/(x^2)$ is not reduced: Cohen-Macaulay is not a smoothness condition.

(b) Let $R$ be regular of dimension $d$ with $\mathfrak m = (x_1,\dots,x_d)$; induct on $d$. For $d = 0$, $R$ is a field. For $d\ge1$: $x_1\neq0$ (otherwise $\mathfrak m$ would be generated by $d-1$ elements, while the number of generators of $\mathfrak m$ is at least $\dim R$), and $R$ is a domain, so $x_1$ is a non-zero-divisor. Then $\dim R/(x_1) = d-1$ (recalled dimension fact) and its maximal ideal is generated by the $d-1$ images of $x_2,\dots,x_d$, so $R/(x_1)$ is regular of dimension $d-1$, hence Cohen-Macaulay by induction. By part 3 of the first-properties theorem, $R$ is Cohen-Macaulay. (Ji, Proposition 2.3, states this without extra hypotheses.)

(c) In a reduced Noetherian ring, $0$ is the intersection of the minimal primes, which is a primary decomposition without embedded components, so the associated primes are the minimal primes. If $\dim R = 1$, then $\mathfrak m$ is not minimal, hence not associated, so $\operatorname{depth}R\ge1 = \dim R$. For the node, $x+y$ is an explicit regular element (Section 1); for the cusp, $t^2$ is a non-zero-divisor in the domain $k[t^2,t^3]$.

(d) $S$ is Cohen-Macaulay by (b), and quotients by regular sequences stay Cohen-Macaulay (part 4 of the first-properties theorem, applied repeatedly with part 2). For $(x^2,yz)$: $x^2\neq0$ in the domain $S$, and $(x^2)$ is $(x)$-primary (if $fg\in(x^2)$ and $f\notin(x)$, then $x^2\mid g$ by unique factorisation), so $\operatorname{Ass}S/(x^2) = \{(x)\}$; as $yz\notin(x)$, so $yz$ is regular on $S/(x^2)$. The quotient has dimension $1$ and is Cohen-Macaulay; Ji gives it as an example.

blocks.title: Three ways to fail
blocks.body: For each ring in the figure, identify which property of Cohen-Macaulay rings fails.
blocks.solution:
(a) $k[x,y]/(x^2,xy)$ at the origin: $\operatorname{Ass} = \{(x),(x,y)\}$ (exercise in the depth section), with $(x,y)$ embedded. Part 1 of the first-properties theorem forbids embedded primes. Equivalently, the depth is $0<1$.

(b) $k[x,y,z]/(xy,xz)$: $\operatorname{Ass} = \{(x),(y,z)\}$, both minimal, but $\dim R/(x) = 2\neq1 = \dim R/(y,z)$. Part 1 requires all associated primes to have $\dim R/\mathfrak p = \dim R$. The ring is reduced but not equidimensional.

(c) $k[w,x,y,z]/((w,x)\cap(y,z))$: reduced, both minimal primes have $\dim R/\mathfrak p = 2$, so part 1 does not detect the failure. Part 4 does: $w+y,\ x+z$ is a system of parameters (modulo it, substituting $y = -w$, $z = -x$, the ideal becomes $(w^2,wx,x^2)$, of finite colength), but it is not a regular sequence, since $R/(w+y)$ has depth $0$ (computed in the previous section) and so $x+z$ is a zero-divisor on it. Wikipedia notes that the failure also follows from Hartshorne's connectedness theorem.

blocks.title: What Cohen-Macaulay means
blocks.body: Five descriptions of the same property of a local ring $R$ (or graded ring), each the working definition in some tradition.

items.label: Depth equals dimension
items.body: $\operatorname{depth}R = \dim R$: the number of independent cuts by non-zero-divisors equals the length of the longest chain of primes. Weibel and the Stacks Project define the notion this way; homological arguments (Ext, Auslander-Buchsbaum) start from it.

items.label: Parameters are independent
items.body: Some, equivalently every, system of parameters is a regular sequence (Hochster's definition). Geometrically: whenever $d = \dim R$ equations cut the space down to a point, they do so as independent equations; this is the form behind the unmixedness theorem of Macaulay and Cohen.

items.label: Local cohomology in one degree
items.body: $H^i_{\mathfrak m}(R) = 0$ for all $i\neq\dim R$. By Weibel 4.6.9 local cohomology lives in degrees between depth and dimension, so this is depth $=$ dimension again; Iyengar-Ma-Schwede-Walker take this vanishing as the definition of big Cohen-Macaulay complexes.

items.label: Free over a polynomial subring
items.body: If $R$ is finite over a regular local (or graded polynomial) subring $A$ of the same dimension, then $R$ is Cohen-Macaulay if and only if $R$ is a free $A$-module ("miracle flatness", Ji Theorem 2.10). Geometrically, for a finite map from an affine variety to affine space of the same dimension, Cohen-Macaulay means every fibre has the same degree; the line with an embedded point has degree $1$ over generic points of the $y$-axis but degree $2$ over $y = 0$.

items.label: Duality
items.body: A scheme is Cohen-Macaulay exactly when its dualizing complex is a single sheaf in one degree, the dualizing sheaf; then Serre duality takes the clean form $\mathrm{Ext}^i(\mathcal F,\omega^\circ_X)\cong H^{n-i}(X,\mathcal F)^\vee$ for all $i$ (Ji, Theorem 3.1, for projective $X$ over an algebraically closed field).

blocks.title: Hidden freeness in the graded case

blocks.body:
We use two facts: graded Nakayama (a finitely generated graded $R$-module $N$ with $N = \mathfrak mN$ is zero, because a homogeneous element of least degree among generators cannot lie in $\mathfrak mN$), and that $A$ is a polynomial ring, i.e. the $\theta_i$ are algebraically independent; the latter holds because $R$ is a finite $A$-module (shown next), so $\dim A = \dim R = d$, and a $k$-algebra generated by $d$ elements has dimension $d$ only if they are algebraically independent.

$R$ is generated as an $A$-module by $b_1,\dots,b_r$. Let $N = \sum_jAb_j$. Then $R = N+(\theta)R$ by the choice of the $b_j$, so the graded $A$-module $R/N$ satisfies $R/N = \sum_i\theta_i(R/N)$. If $R/N\neq0$, a non-zero homogeneous element of least degree cannot lie in $\sum_i\theta_i(R/N)$, whose homogeneous elements of that degree come from elements of strictly smaller degree, since every $\theta_i$ has positive degree. So $R/N = 0$.

2 implies 1. $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_d$ is regular on the polynomial ring $A$, hence on any free $A$-module $A^r$ (componentwise), and $R/(\theta)R\neq0$.

1 implies 2. Induct on $d$; for $d = 0$, $R$ is finite-dimensional with basis $b_j$. Let $d\ge1$ and suppose $\sum_ja_jb_j = 0$ with homogeneous $a_j\in A$ (of degrees making the sum homogeneous), not all zero, chosen with $\max\deg a_j$ minimal. Put $R' = R/\theta_dR$: it is graded, $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_{d-1}$ is a homogeneous system of parameters of $R'$ that is $R'$-regular, and $R'/(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_{d-1})R' = R/(\theta)R$, with the images $\bar b_j$ as basis. By induction $R'$ is free over $A' = k[\theta_1,\dots,\theta_{d-1}]$ with basis $\bar b_j$. Reducing the relation modulo $\theta_d$ (which sends $A = A'[\theta_d]$ onto $A'$) gives $\sum_j\bar a_j\bar b_j = 0$, so every $\bar a_j = 0$, i.e. $a_j = \theta_da_j'$. Then $\theta_d\sum_ja_j'b_j = 0$, and since $\theta_d$ is a non-zero-divisor on $R$, $\sum_ja'_jb_j = 0$, a non-trivial relation of smaller degree. This contradiction shows the $b_j$ are a basis.

1 implies 3. The $\theta_i$ lie in $\mathfrak m$, so they stay regular in $R_{\mathfrak m}$ (localisation of regular sequences), giving $\operatorname{depth}R_{\mathfrak m}\ge d = \dim R_{\mathfrak m}$.

3 implies 1. The images of the $\theta_i$ form a system of parameters of $R_{\mathfrak m}$, so they are $R_{\mathfrak m}$-regular by part 4 of the first-properties theorem. Let $N$ be one of the graded modules $R/(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_{i-1})R$ and $K$ the kernel of $\theta_i$ on $N$, a graded submodule with $K_{\mathfrak m} = 0$. For homogeneous $a\in K$, some $s\notin\mathfrak m$ has $sa = 0$; the degree-$0$ component of $s$ is a non-zero scalar $c$, and as $a$ is homogeneous, $ca = 0$ (compare the components of $sa$ in degree $\deg a$). So $a = 0$, $K = 0$, and $\theta_i$ is a non-zero-divisor on $N$.

blocks.title: Monomial curves and hidden freeness
blocks.body: (a) Show that $R = k[t^3,t^4,t^5]\subseteq k[t]$ is a free module over $A = k[t^3]$ and find a basis. (b) Show that $R = k[x,y]/(x^2,xy)$ is not free over $A = k[y]$, although $y$ is a homogeneous system of parameters.
blocks.solution:
(a) $R$ has $k$-basis $t^s$ with $s$ in the semigroup $S = \langle3,4,5\rangle = \{0,3,4,5,6,7,\dots\}$ (all integers except $1,2$). $t^3$ is a homogeneous system of parameters: $R/t^3R$ has basis $t^s$, $s\in S\setminus(3+S)$, and $3+S = \{3,6,7,8,\dots\}$, so $S\setminus(3+S) = \{0,4,5\}$ and $\dim_kR/t^3R = 3$. Since $R$ is a domain, $t^3$ is a non-zero-divisor, so by the theorem $1,t^4,t^5$ is an $A$-basis: $R = A\oplus At^4\oplus At^5$. Concretely, every $s\in S$ is uniquely $3j+b$ with $b\in\{0,4,5\}$, $j\ge0$ (the three residues mod $3$, each starting at its smallest element of $S$), as in the figure. In particular the Hilbert series is $(1+t^4+t^5)/(1-t^3)$.

(b) $R$ has $k$-basis $1,x,y,y^2,\dots$ (all $y^j$ and $x$). $R/yR = k[x]/(x^2)$ is finite-dimensional, so $y$ is a homogeneous system of parameters ($\dim R = 1$). $R = A\cdot1+k\cdot x$, and $yx = 0$, so $x$ is a non-zero torsion element and $R$ is not free. Equivalently $y$ is not regular, and $R_{\mathfrak m}$ has depth $0$. In the terms of the fibre-degree criterion: the fibre of $\operatorname{Spec}R\to\operatorname{Spec}k[y]$ over $y = c\neq0$ is $k[x]/(x)$ after localising, of degree $1$, but over $y = 0$ it is $k[x]/(x^2)$, of degree $2$.

blocks.caption: The exponents of $k[t^3,t^4,t^5]$ (the semigroup $\langle3,4,5\rangle$) split into three progressions $b+3\mathbb N$ with $b = 0,4,5$: this is the decomposition $R = A\oplus At^4\oplus At^5$ over $A = k[t^3]$.
